q: The primary distinction between ABC recording and functional analysis is that:
choices: A. Functional analysis requires more trained staff to run its conditions
B. ABC recording shows correlation; functional analysis shows causation
C. ABC recording is valid only for escape-maintained behavior
D. ABC recording uses shorter observation intervals than analog sessions

q: Using indirect assessment alone to design a restrictive behavior intervention plan is problematic primarily because:
choices: A. It violates an IDEA mandate that functional analysis precede every BIP
B. It fails the BACB standard that assessment fit the presenting problem
C. Indirect assessment cannot be conducted in naturalistic settings
D. Indirect assessments are not recognized by insurance funders

q: A high-probability (high-p) request sequence builds compliance primarily by:
choices: A. Altering stimulus control with a run of reinforced compliance
B. Abolishing the motivating operation for escape from demands
C. Changing reinforcer value through deprivation before the demand
D. Delivering noncontingent attention on a fixed-time schedule

q: A setting event differs from a discriminative stimulus primarily in that a setting event:
choices: A. Functions as a conditioned reinforcer for appropriate behavior
B. Is always an internal biological state rather than an environmental event
C. Alters the probability of behavior without directly evoking it
D. Directly evokes the problem behavior at the moment it is presented

q: The primary advantage of semi-logarithmic (Standard Celeration Chart) display over standard equal-interval graphs is that:
choices: A. It is the only display format that supports visual analysis
B. It shows proportional rate changes as equal vertical distances
C. It eliminates session-to-session variability from the data path
D. It is easier to construct by hand than equal-interval paper

q: A generalized conditioned reinforcer remains effective across many different states of deprivation and satiation because it:
choices: A. Functions as an unconditioned reinforcer once pairing is complete
B. Is exchanged for a single highly preferred backup reinforcer
C. Is paired with many different backups and does not depend on one MO
D. Is biologically significant to the species without a learning history

q: Evaluation of a behavior-change procedure's side effects should include:
choices: A. Only effects that caregivers spontaneously report to the analyst
B. Effects on the target behavior alone, tracked across sessions
C. Adverse and beneficial collateral effects, measured directly
D. Only effects that increase the rate of the problem behavior

q: Behavioral momentum theory holds that resistance to change is primarily a function of:
choices: A. The topography and effort of the response being measured
B. The density of the punishment schedule currently in effect
C. The rate of reinforcement correlated with the stimulus context
D. The response-reinforcer contingency arranged for the target response

q: Which definition of elopement best satisfies the objective, clear, and complete tests?
choices: A. Crossing the marked classroom threshold unaccompanied
B. Any attempt to escape or elope from the classroom area
C. Wandering off from the group because he is feeling anxious
D. Leaving the area at any time without adult permission

q: A clinician establishes a new tact in massed discrete trials, then moves to capturing the response during play to promote generalization. This sequence reflects:
choices: A. A procedural error, because discrete-trial and free-operant formats cannot be combined
B. A changing criterion design, with play serving as the new response criterion
C. Multiple-treatment interference confounding the two teaching arrangements
D. Discrete-trial acquisition followed by free-operant teaching for generalization

q: The principal threat to interpretation when two treatments alternate rapidly within a multielement design is:
choices: A. Regression to the mean across repeated measures
B. Observer drift across the study's later sessions
C. Insufficient trials to reach the mastery criterion
D. Multiple-treatment interference across conditions

q: In an ABAB design, experimental control is demonstrated when:
choices: A. Behavior fails to reverse when the intervention is withdrawn
B. Behavior covaries with the IV across all phase changes
C. The IV is introduced at least three separate times
D. Behavior improves during the first B phase of the design only

q: A student sees a classmate praised for raising her hand and begins doing so the next day. This is:
choices: A. Observational learning through vicarious reinforcement
B. Echoic behavior under formal similarity to the model
C. Generalized imitation of a novel, untrained motor model
D. Imitation, because the response topographies match the model

q: One behavioral mechanism by which a signed contingency contract increases follow-through is that:
choices: A. It acts as a contingency-specifying rule and recruits social consequences
B. It converts a skill deficit into a performance deficit without direct teaching
C. It prevents the individual from helping negotiate the terms or criterion
D. It removes any need to actually deliver the reinforcer specified in the contract

q: Response generalization in behavior reduction contexts is clinically significant because:
choices: A. New topographies may emerge within the same response class
B. It removes the need for extinction in differential reinforcement
C. It guarantees that FCT responses transfer to new settings
D. It removes any need to program multiple exemplar training

q: In visual analysis of single-case data, 'overlap' between adjacent phases refers to:
choices: A. The similarity of variability between two adjacent conditions
B. The number of data points shared across the two adjacent conditions
C. The degree to which the trend lines of adjacent phases intersect
D. The proportion of points falling within the adjacent phase's range

q: A CMO-T (transitive conditioned motivating operation) is best described as:
choices: A. A stimulus whose presence makes something else a reinforcer
B. An establishing operation requiring no learning history
C. A stimulus paired with another MO whose effects it acquires
D. A stimulus that has been paired with a worsening of conditions

q: When a multiple relationship cannot be avoided (for example, in a small rural community), the Ethics Code directs the behavior analyst to:
choices: A. Take steps to mitigate the risk, starting with clarifying roles
B. Transfer ethical responsibility to the client's caregivers
C. Immediately terminate all services and refer the client elsewhere
D. Proceed without documenting or clarifying the overlapping roles

q: A token economy without a fading plan is problematic primarily because:
choices: A. Behavior stays dependent on tokens rather than natural reinforcers
B. Token economies cannot be run in naturalistic community settings
C. The exchange schedule is legally required to thin over time
D. It violates the least-restrictive-alternative principle in the Code

q: In an A-B-A-B, responding changes immediately at every phase change with no overlap between adjacent phases. This shows:
choices: A. Regression to the mean across the four repeated conditions
B. Strong experimental control across replicated conditions
C. Poor social validity, since the change was abrupt
D. A Type II error produced by excessive baseline variability

q: A multiple baseline design demonstrates experimental control by:
choices: A. Withdrawing the IV and showing the behavior reverses to baseline
B. Raising the reinforcement criterion in successive graduated steps
C. Comparing two interventions head-to-head in the same phase
D. Showing that behavior changes only when the IV reaches that tier

q: Non-contingent reinforcement (NCR) reduces problem behavior primarily by:
choices: A. Increasing the response effort required for problem behavior
B. Abolishing the MO for the behavior's maintaining reinforcer
C. Establishing the alternative response as the new SD
D. Punishing the problem behavior each time it is emitted
